title: What Is a Headless CMS and Why Should You Care
excerpt: "Headless CMS" sounds like developer jargon. It isn't. Here's what it means, why it matters for your business, and when you actually need one.

blocks.text: If you've spent any time reading about modern web development, you've probably come across "headless CMS." It shows up in agency pitches, in tech blogs, in feature comparisons. And it's almost always explained in ways that lose non-technical readers immediately.
Here's the business-owner version. What a headless CMS is, what problem it was designed to solve, what it costs, and — most importantly — whether your business actually needs one.
What Is a CMS?

Let's start at the beginning. CMS stands for Content Management System. It's software that lets you create, edit, and publish content on a website without writing code. WordPress is the most common example. Joomla, Drupal, TYPO3, Squarespace — all CMS platforms.

A traditional CMS does two jobs at once: it stores your content (in a database), and it renders that content into web pages. When a visitor loads your page, the CMS grabs the content from the database, applies a template, and sends the assembled HTML to the browser.
For most of the web's history, this worked fine. Write it once, display it once, on your website.
What Makes a CMS "Headless"?

A headless CMS keeps the content management side — the editing interface, the content storage, the workflow tools — but removes the rendering side. It doesn't generate HTML pages for visitors. It has no "head" (no front end).

Instead, a headless CMS exposes your content as structured data via an API. Any application — a website, a mobile app, a smart TV interface, a digital kiosk — can connect to that API, pull the content, and display it however it needs to.
The CMS stores and manages the content. The front-end application decides how it looks.

Think of it like a supplier and a retailer. The headless CMS is the supplier: it has the inventory system, manages quality, and fulfills orders. The retailer (your website, your app, your partner portal) decides how to present those goods to customers. Different retailers can all draw from the same supplier.

Why the Headless Model Exists
Headless emerged because the web changed. In 2010, most people browsed on a desktop. You published to one website, and that was it.

Today, content needs to reach mobile apps, tablets, voice interfaces, digital signage, TV apps, and partner integrations — all from a single source of truth. A traditional CMS wasn't built for this. You end up manually duplicating content across systems with no clean way to keep things in sync.

Headless also unlocked serious performance gains. When content lives in a headless CMS and the front end is built with a modern framework like Next.js, pages can be pre-rendered as static HTML and served from a global CDN. The result is load times in the 100–300ms range — fast enough to measurably affect conversions.
Real Business Reasons to Go Headless
1. You publish to multiple channels

Write a product description once in your CMS. It automatically appears on your website, in your iOS app, in your Android app, in your partner portal, and on your in-store digital screens. Change it in one place, it updates everywhere. For businesses managing large content catalogs across platforms, this is a genuine efficiency gain.
2. You need proper editorial workflow tools

Purpose-built headless CMSs like Sanity and Contentful have editorial features that WordPress's core doesn't match natively: structured content types, custom workflows, approval stages, full version history, content scheduling, inline commenting, and rich localization support. These aren't plugins bolted on — they're how the system was designed from the start.
3. Your front end needs to evolve independently

With a traditional CMS, redesigning your site often means migrating your content as well. With a headless setup, your content stays put in the CMS and only the front end changes. If you want to rebuild your website in three years without touching your content structure, headless makes that significantly easier.
4. Performance at scale

Headless architectures pair naturally with static generation. Pre-rendered pages served from CDN don't hit a server for every visitor request. For high-traffic sites where page speed directly correlates with revenue, this architecture removes a bottleneck that plugins and server-side rendering can't fully solve.
The Real Costs of Going Headless
None of this is free. Here's what going headless actually costs:
More moving parts

You're maintaining a CMS subscription, a separate front-end codebase, and the integration layer between them. When something breaks, there's more surface area to debug. Two systems means two potential failure points.
Developer setup is required

You can't install a headless stack and have a working website in an afternoon. The integration — connecting the CMS API to your front-end framework, setting up content models, configuring preview — takes real development work. Expect €3,000–€8,000 or more to set up properly, depending on scope.
CMS subscription costs

Enterprise headless CMSs aren't free at scale. Contentful's basic paid plan starts at around €300/month. Sanity has a free tier that works for small projects, with team plans starting around €99/month. These costs compound over time and need to be factored into the total cost of ownership.
Preview requires extra work

Live preview — seeing how your content looks before publishing — is built into WordPress. In a headless setup, you need to build or configure preview functionality explicitly. It's solvable, but it's not free.
Popular Headless CMS Options
If you're evaluating headless CMSs, here's a practical reference:

items: **Sanity** — Highly customizable, excellent developer experience, real-time collaboration. Free tier available. Good for teams that want full control over their content model.
**Contentful** — Enterprise-grade, strong localization, mature ecosystem. More expensive at scale. Common in larger organizations.
**Storyblok** — Visual editor that feels closer to a page builder. Lower barrier for non-technical editors.
**Payload CMS** — Open-source, self-hosted, built on Node.js. Avoids SaaS costs and keeps your data on your own infrastructure.
**Directus** — Open-source, wraps any SQL database, free to self-host. More of a data platform than a pure CMS, but very flexible.

blocks.text: When You Don't Need a Headless CMS
Be honest here. Most small and mid-sized business websites don't need headless architecture. You probably don't need it if:

items: You have one website and no plans for a mobile app
Your content team is one or two people
You publish new content infrequently — a few times a month
You're not publishing the same content to multiple channels
You need fast time-to-launch with a limited budget

blocks.text: Adding headless to a simple business website is engineering overhead that buys you nothing. It's the equivalent of installing a commercial kitchen in a studio apartment because you once read that professional chefs use it.
When It Genuinely Makes Sense
You should seriously consider headless when:

items: You're publishing to multiple platforms (web + app + other surfaces) and manual syncing is already painful
Your editorial team has outgrown WordPress's workflow tools
You have strict performance requirements and need sub-second load times globally
You're building a product — not just a marketing site — where content management is a core feature
You have dedicated development capacity to build and maintain the integration

blocks.text: A Note on File-Based Content

There's a third option that often gets left out of the headless conversation: storing content directly in the codebase as structured files (JSON or Markdown). No CMS subscription, no API to maintain, no additional moving parts.

For business sites with relatively stable content — service pages, case studies, a blog — this approach is simple, fast, and version-controlled. It's what we use for most sites we build. When clients want to update content, they email us, and most updates are processed and deployed automatically within minutes.

It's not right for every situation — a large editorial team with daily publishing needs something more sophisticated. But it eliminates a lot of complexity for clients who don't need a full CMS workflow.
How We Approach This at webvise
Our default stack is Next.js with file-based content — no CMS required. This covers the vast majority of our clients' needs without the overhead.

For clients who genuinely need headless — multi-channel publishing, a large editorial team, complex content modeling, or localization workflows — we integrate Sanity or Contentful with the same Next.js front end. Editors get a clean, purpose-built interface. The site performs like a statically generated site because it is one.
The architecture follows the actual requirement. Not the other way around.
The Short Version

A headless CMS stores and manages your content but delegates rendering to a separate front-end application. It enables multi-channel publishing, better performance, and more flexible editorial workflows — but adds cost and complexity.
Most small business websites don't need it. High-traffic sites, multi-platform products, and large editorial operations often do.
